# 1. Executive Summary {#1}

a\) **The paradox.**

b\) **A success that is strategically misfocused.** The Indian software
story is a genuine success --- \$283bn revenue; it is a short-term,
opportunistic commercial win built on the cost advantage of application
development and support.

c\) **Products built for export, not for home.** India\'s product and IP
efforts ([]{#O1_ZOHO}[Zoho](https://www.zoho.com/aboutus.html),
[]{#O1_FRSHWK}[Freshworks](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/FRSH/),
[]{#O1_POSTMN}[Postman](https://www.postman.com/company/about-postman/),
[]{#O1_BRWSTK}[BrowserStack](https://www.browserstack.com/about)) serve
export markets --- domestic revenue is \~10--20%. East Asian champions
([]{#O1_ALIBAB}[Alibaba](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/BABA/),
[]{#O1_TENCNT}[Tencent](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/TCEHY/),
[]{#O1_NAVER}[Naver](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/NHNCF/),
[]{#O1_KAKAO}[Kakao](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/035720.KS/)) were
built domestic-first (\~70--90% home revenue) and exported only later.
Are we building for someone else\'s problem?

d\) **A different path elsewhere.** Other countries, notably China,
treat the foundational layer as strategic and pursue import substitution
by policy: the IOE-replacement drive
([]{#O1_IBM}[IBM](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/IBM/),
[]{#O1_ORACLE}[Oracle](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/ORCL/),
[]{#O1_EMC}[EMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMC_Corporation)) and a
captive domestic market produced []{#T1_POLRDB}[PolarDB
Limitless](https://github.com/ApsaraDB/PolarDB-for-PostgreSQL) (2,055M
tpmC, a 2025 TPC-C world record),
[]{#T1_TDSQL}[TDSQL](https://cloud.tencent.com/product/tdsql),
[]{#T1_OCBASE}[OceanBase](https://github.com/oceanbase/oceanbase),
[]{#T1_HARMOS}[HarmonyOS](https://www.openharmony.cn/), and
[]{#T1_OPNEUR}[openEuler](https://openeuler.org/) --- sovereign stacks
built deliberately, not accidentally.

e\) **The floor, and the renter.** This essay abstracts foundational
software as \"the floor\". I also theorize i) Owning the floor is a
strategic asset ii) India has not focused on this iii) There are
exceptions and recent signs are encouraging

f\) **The exceptions --- and how they were built.** India did produce
builders, but the approach is in contrast with how China has approached
a similar situation of being a renter China: When [Ant Financial](#3.5)
--- a *user* of Oracle database, faced a fundamental challenge it built
OceanBase from scratch: new storage engine, new consensus, new
everything over a 10-year horizon India: Business users building from
scratch is rare. Recent developments at []{#O1_NPCI}[National Payments
Corporation of India (NPCI)](https://www.npci.org.in/about-us) and
consistent efforts at
[]{#O1_ZERODH}[Zerodha](https://zerodha.com/about/) and
[]{#O1_PHONPE}[PhonePe](https://www.phonepe.com/en/about.html) are
noteworthy. [*Author\'s Judgement*]{.spurious-link target="D1_AJ"}
India: [YugabyteDB](#3.7), a *software company* rather than a user, took
a similar problem and answered it by assembly: it kept what worked (the
PostgreSQL query engine, reused almost intact) and built only what was
missing (DocDB, the distributed storage layer, plus Raft consensus). The
Indian anti-pattern to my theory are i) [Zoho/AdventNet](#5.2.2) in its
earlier avatar when it worked on SNMP ii) {{{O1~ZERODH~}}}\'s
[]{#T1_KAFRLY}[kaf-relay](https://github.com/zerodha/kaf-relay) and
[]{#T1_DUNGBT}[DungBeetle](https://github.com/zerodha/dungbeetle) iii)
[PhonePe Drove](#6.7) --- the Mesos replacement and I like the
documentation iv)
[]{#T1_KITTY}[Kitty](https://github.com/kovidgoyal/kitty) --- I do not
use it, but my []{#T1_WEZTRM}[WezTerm](https://github.com/wez/wezterm)
terminal uses its protocols v)
[]{#T1_MINIO}[MinIO](https://github.com/minio/minio) and its earlier
version vi) []{#T1_ERPNXT}[ERPNext](https://github.com/frappe/erpnext) -
the ERP that I use, and the []{#T1_FRAPPE}[Frappe
Framework](https://github.com/frappe/frappe) that read about All real
and fascinating work --- but exceptions, not an ecosystem.

g\) **Why the exceptions never compound.** The traction of India\'s
floor-builders is lost because policy and mindset support none of the
five patterns by which foundational software gets built --- i) obsessive
lone wolf or a pack ii) mass community driven iii) institutional
commission with a vision and resources iv) specialist tools v) and
scale-problem-that-refuses-workarounds [Section 6.2.3](#6.2.3) explores
these patterns.

h\) **Missed opportunities.** i) Government: The 1990s
[]{#O1_CDAC}[Centre for Development of Advanced Computing
(C-DAC)](https://www.cdac.in/index.aspx?id=about) developed, supplied,
and exported PARAM supercomputers. This involved proprietary primitives:
a) Network Interconnects b) remote memory management c) parallel
distributed filesystem and checkpoint-restart A successful product and
ancillary solutions existed inside C-DAC. These were foundational work
equivalent to e.g., a) [Huawei](#6.4.2)\'s
`drivers/net/ethernet/hisilicon/`{.verbatim} and
`drivers/crypto/hisilicon/`{.verbatim}, or b)
[]{#O1_SANDIA}[Sandia](https://www.sandia.gov/about/) and
[]{#O1_OAKRDG}[Oak Ridge](https://www.ornl.gov/) seeded
`fs/lustre/`{.verbatim} c) the RDMA subsystem
[]{#O1_MELLNX}[Mellanox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellanox_Technologies)/[]{#O1_NVIDIA}[NVIDIA](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/NVDA/)
now dominates. Technology changes affected C-DAC\'s evolution. We do
believe the technology could have been selectively open sourced. We
could have had some reference hardware.

ii\) Private: Zoho/AdventNet\'s stated position to build an OS has its
roots in its []{#T1_SNMP}[Simple Network Management Protocol
(SNMP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Network_Management_Protocol)/[]{#T1_WEBNMS}[WebNMS](https://www.webnms.com/)
legacy. I see little effort in Zoho to build a community around its
software. The [Ulaa
browser](https://ulaabrowser.zohodesk.in/portal/en/community/ulaa)
initiative --- with both open-source and proprietary closed branches ---
would help adoption and ecosystem building. Zoho\'s strategy of being
closed source and less community driven has definitely worked
commercially. This strategic choice, however, does limit ecosystem
formation.

Both failures [*Author\'s Judgement*]{.spurious-link target="D1_AJ"} are
of governance and ecosystem support, not of talent. My criteria for
failure is \"Adoption of foundational software developed by an
Organization\" , this is a qualitative call.

i\) **Strategy versus Jugaad.** It is not that India never hit the wall.

i\) PhonePe hit it when []{#T1_AMESOS}[Apache
Mesos](https://attic.apache.org/projects/mesos.html) (moved to Apache
Attic, 2024) could no longer run its clusters, and built [Drove](#6.7)
to replace it
([]{#T1_DROVE}[github.com/PhonePe/drove-orchestrator](https://github.com/PhonePe/drove-orchestrator)).

ii\) Zerodha hit it in its reporting layer and built DungBeetle.

However the characteristic Indian answer is to assemble, extend, or rent
--- recombine what already works --- rather than to build the floor from
scratch. China\'s answer to the same class of wall was OceanBase: a
from-scratch, sovereign build. Jugaad wins the quarter; ownership wins
the decade.

The choice to be a renter or not is not just an economic decision. There
is a \"Strategic Independence\" decision in the loop. The logical flow
is not disturbed even if you ignore the red-bordered items of the
Decision Algorithm. I do believe this has happened in the case of India
and, combined with the \"The Collective Problem\" I theorize below, we
are in a unique situation.

> **The Collective Problem**
>
> When everyone follows the rational algorithm, the collective outcome
> is capability atrophy.

j\) **The protocol triumph --- and its limit.** []{#T1_UPI}[Unified
Payments Interface
(UPI)](https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/product-overview) (\~500
million transactions a day, \~₹314 lakh crore a year, roughly half the
world\'s real-time payments),
[]{#T1_AADHAR}[Aadhaar](https://uidai.gov.in/en/about-uidai/unique-identification-authority-of-india.html)
(\~1.3 billion enrolled), []{#T1_ONDC}[Open Network for Digital Commerce
(ONDC)](https://ondc.org/about-ondc/) and []{#T1_ABHA}[Ayushman Bharat
Health Account (ABHA)](https://abdm.gov.in/abha) are genuine
achievements of system-level thinking.

The genesis is the excellent work of []{#O1_ISPIRT}[Indian Software
Product Industry Round Table (iSPIRT)](https://ispirt.in/): 3 API layers
(Identity, Payments, Data) or 4 evolutionary layers (Presence-less,
Paperless, Cashless, Consent). Design and systems thinking overcame the
legacy problems of the administrative setup. I hope that problem-solving
approach compounds. Even though this is not foundational software work,
it is thinking from scratch, bottom-up, not starting with a Jugaad
jacket and force fitting.

But they are a protocol floor propped up by policy and mandate, not a
technology floor: India defined the APIs, standards and identity layers
while renting the databases, runtimes and message brokers beneath them.

k\) **The target.** We propose a Made-in-India stack with a falsifiable
target: by 2030, at least one globally adopted foundational project
originated and neutrally governed from India. The approach is
institutional, not rhetorical: (i) an Indian Open Source Foundation to
hold IP in neutral custody; (ii) an upstream-first mandate making
government-funded software ([C-DAC](#6.4.4.3), []{#O1_CDOT}[Centre for
Development of Telematics
(C-DOT)](https://www.cdot.in/cdotweb/web/aboutUs.jsp)) open by default;
(iii) MSME-cluster tooling built with local polytechnics on 3--5-year
horizons; (iv) an Indian-language data corpus; and (v) one 20-year,
government-commissioned foundational project --- a distributed,
tamper-resistant land-records system, open from day one.

# 3. Discovery Story --- How I Decided to Explore This Area {#3}

## 3.1. The CBDC Question {#3.1}

My work in pilot phase of Indian Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)
made me explore DBs that can be used. Oracle was the standard and
startups were adopting
[]{#T1_POSTGR}[PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/about/). I decided
to do a literature scan and questioned \"What is the best Database to
use for our CBDC app?\" . The result was surprising.

  Alibaba PolarDB Limitless    2,055M   PolarDB MySQL 8.0   Jan 2025
  Tencent TDSQL (1650 nodes)   815M     TDSQL v10.3         Mar 2023
  Alibaba OceanBase ECS #1     707M     OceanBase v2.2      May 2020
  Alibaba OceanBase ECS #2     61M      OceanBase v2.2      Oct 2019

Oracle, (our DB) was 5th at 30M tpmC and I did not find PostgreSQL or
any other OSS.

## 3.2. Realization: Chinese DBs Are Ruling TPC {#3.2}

1.  Alibaba / Ant dominates the TPC. Enquiry into the systems used
    revealed, its a sovereign stack; every component self-developed:
    -   DB: PolarDB for MySQL 8.0

        ::: {.NOTE .drawer}
        PolarDB is a drop-in replacement for MySQL 8.0 apps.
        :::

    -   OS: Paladin (custom Linux)

    -   CPU: []{#T1_YITIAN}[Yitian
        710](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitian_710) (5nm, 128 ARM
        cores)

    -   Server: Panjiu

    -   Network: ICN Switch
2.  Tencent\'s DB, OS, and cluster management are all self-developed.

The playbook is similar to Western Enterprise Linux OS\'s vendors\'
playbook. a) begin with opensource b) add features + do fundamental
development with opensource as base c) develop community d) give most
back + keep some This is happening at time when traditional western
opensource vendors are taking opensource offline. So I see in China a
general approach a) opensource is the **foundation**, not the product.

-   OceanBase is opensourced (Mulan PL);
-   Paladin, []{#T1_ANOLIS}[Aliyun Linux](https://openanolis.cn/),
    []{#T1_TLINUX}[tlinux](https://github.com/Tencent/TencentOS-kernel)
    all derive from community Linux.

b\) the product is the add-ons

-   cluster orchestration,
-   hardware integration,
-   and software-hardware co-design

and are proprietary.The Chinese companies are **extending and
controlling** open source to build a sovereign floor.

  System                      tpmC     Self-Developed Components
  --------------------------- -------- -----------------------------------------
  Alibaba PolarDB Limitless   2,055M   DB + OS + CPU + Server + Network
  Tencent TDSQL               815M     DB + OS + Cluster Management
  Alibaba OceanBase           707M     DB + OS (DB open-sourced 2021, MulanPL)

  : Top 3 TPC-C --- Self-Developed Stack Components
  {#Tab.TPC_Top3_Results}

**Source: TPC-C official results** [TPC-C
Results](https://www.tpc.org/tpcc/results/tpcc_results5.asp?print=false&orderby=tpm&sortby=desc)

## 3.3. Wonder: Open-Source DBs Are Not There {#3.3}

Open-source databases are absent because TPC-C submission is expensive:

-   Hundreds of nodes of hardware investment.
-   Engineering time to tune the full stack: OS, DB, networking,
    storage.
-   An independent audit, adding substantial fees.

No community project has the commercial incentive to spend millions just
to publish a number. This does not mean open-source databases are
untested. The community uses:

-   **HammerDB**: open-source TPROC-C/TPROC-H tool; supports PostgreSQL,
    MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, MariaDB.
-   **Sysbench**: multi-threaded benchmark supporting MySQL and
    PostgreSQL.
-   **DBT-2 / DBT-5**: open-source implementations of TPC-C / TPC-E.

Representative HammerDB TPROC-C on single-node AMD EPYC with NVMe:

-   PostgreSQL 16: \~600,000 NOPM
-   MySQL 8.0: \~400,000 NOPM

The gap is not software capability but the cost of submission --- a
formal TPC-C audit runs to millions of dollars. Open-source databases
perform reasonably; they simply do not publish rankings. [*Author\'s
Judgement*]{.spurious-link target="D1_AJ"}

## 3.4. Who Made PolarDB? What Other DBs Have They Made? {#3.4}

Alibaba was a standard Oracle shop in 2007. Singles' Day (11.11) ---
China's annual online shopping festival --- created a forcing function:
transaction volumes spiked 100× in hours, exposing Oracle's vertical
scaling limits. Alibaba initiated OceanBase in 2010 (first deployed for
Taobao Favourites, 2011); Ant Financial adopted it as its core database.
By 2014, OceanBase handled \~10% of Alipay's 11.11 traffic --- a live
proof of concept alongside Oracle, not a replacement. The payment system
moved fully off Oracle in 2015; core accounting followed in 2016.
OceanBase was open-sourced in 2021 under MulanPubL-2.0 and relicensed to
Apache-2.0 in March 2026. PolarDB launched in 2018 as a cloud- native
MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible engine. PolarDB Limitless set the TPC-C
world record in January 2025.

> The intent behind this 18-year programme was not to win a benchmark.
> Ant now owns its most strategic infrastructure asset end to end ---
> permanently. The database is not a vendor relationship; it is the
> floor. The only remaining risk: a competitor that builds a better
> database and anchors superior user experience from the tech side alone
> --- a risk Ant can at least see coming, because they own the floor.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-ant-db-lineage
//| fig-cap: "Alibaba / Ant Group — Database evolution 2007–2025"
{
const ant_db = [
  {year: 2007, label: "Oracle (rented)", event: "Oracle dependency", hi: 1},
  {year: 2010, label: "OceanBase v1", event: "Self-built RDBMS", hi: -1},
  {year: 2014, label: "OceanBase v1.x", event: "Singles’ Day: Oracle-free", hi: 1},
  {year: 2017, label: "OceanBase v2.0", event: "MySQL-compat", hi: -1},
  {year: 2018, label: "PolarDB v1", event: "Cloud-native launch", hi: 1},
  {year: 2021, label: "OceanBase OSS", event: "Open-sourced (MulanPubL-2.0)", hi: -1},
  {year: 2025, label: "PolarDB Limitless", event: "TPC-C record: 2,055M tpmC", hi: 1}
];

return Plot.plot({

  marginBottom: 80,

  },

## 3.5. OceanBase Is Open-Sourced --- What Else Is Ant Building? {#3.5}

Ant's stack is deliberately multi-language: each layer uses the language
whose properties match its requirements. None of these components were
built for external consumption --- they emerged from production
necessity. Open-sourcing is a consequence, not the motivation.

  Layer                      Language   Rationale
  -------------------------- ---------- ------------------------------------
  Application / middleware   Java       JVM tooling; ecosystem depth
  Network proxy / sidecar    Go         Goroutines; single binary
  Database internals         C++        Manual memory; no GC holding locks
  Kernel / crypto / TEE      Rust       Memory safety without GC
  Data / ML pipelines        Python     Ecosystem; not latency-critical

  : Ant Group --- Language by Layer {#Tab.Ant_Lang_By_Layer}

  Component    Primary Function                        Open-Source
  ------------ --------------------------------------- --------------------------------
  SOFABoot     Spring Boot base; class isolation       Yes (Apache 2.0)
  SOFARPC      Inter-service RPC; Bolt over Netty      Yes (Apache 2.0)
  SOFABolt     Binary RPC transport; custom framing    Yes (Apache 2.0)
  SOFAJRaft    Raft consensus; used in OceanBase       Yes (Apache 2.0)
  SOFAArk      Classloader isolation; version safety   Yes (Apache 2.0)
  SOFATracer   Distributed tracing; traceId flow       Yes (Apache 2.0)
  Seata        Distributed txn: AT / TCC / Saga        Yes (Apache TLP)
  RocketMQ     Transactional message queue             Yes (Apache TLP)
  Nacos        Service discovery and config            Yes (Apache TLP)
  MOSN         Go sidecar proxy; xDS; vs Envoy         Yes (Apache 2.0)
  Layotto      Dapr-compatible app runtime (Go)        Yes (Apache 2.0)
  OceanBase    Distributed HTAP RDBMS; TPC-C #1        Yes (MulanPubL-2.0→Apache-2.0)
  TuGraph      Graph DB; fraud detection (C++)         Yes
  Asterinas    Rust OS kernel; Linux ABI               Yes
  Occlum       Library OS for Intel SGX (Rust)         Yes
  Tongsuo      OpenSSL fork; SM2/SM3/SM4 (C)           Yes
  SecretFlow   Privacy-preserving ML; federated        Yes

  : Ant Group Open-Source Infrastructure Stack
  {#Tab.Ant_Stack_Components}

Not open-sourced (the proprietary moat):

-   LDC routing: how transactions are pinned to their zone
-   Unit-based partitioning: user sharding across IDCs
-   Production GC tuning configs at Singles' Day scale
-   Internal risk and fraud model weights

## 3.6. General Appreciation of Foundational Software Work in China {#3.6}

The databases and middleware from Ant are one visible slice of a much
broader pattern. Across China, technology companies have built and
open-sourced foundational infrastructure at a scale that has no Indian
equivalent.

-   Tencent's TDSQL and TBase distributed engine,
-   Alibaba's
    []{#T1_RCKTMQ}[RocketMQ](https://github.com/apache/rocketmq) (now an
    Apache top-level project),
-   []{#O1_HUAWEI}[Huawei](https://www.huawei.com/en/corporate-information)'s
    []{#T1_OPGAUS}[openGauss](https://github.com/opengauss-mirror/openGauss-server)
    (PostgreSQL-compatible, open-sourced in 2020),
-   []{#O1_BYTDNC}[ByteDance](https://www.bytedance.com/en/about)'s
    ByteKV, and
-   []{#O1_PINGCP}[PingCAP](https://www.pingcap.com/about/)'s
    []{#T1_TIDB}[TiDB](https://github.com/pingcap/tidb)---each emerged
    from internal necessity and eventually

became public infrastructure.

Similarly

-   Huawei's OpenHarmony is an attempt at a sovereign OS kernel.
-   Alibaba's Anolis OS is an Opensource Linux, stress-tested at
    hyperscale.

These are not academic projects; they were hardened under production
loads that dwarf most Western deployments.

::: aside
[]{#T1_GITEE}[Gitee](https://gitee.com) --- China\'s domestic code forge
--- is a story for [Section 6.4](#6.4). I loved the [learn-git-branching
game on Gitee](https://help.gitee.com/learn-Git-Branching/) for its
intuitive approach to branching. I am in the middle of another article
on my experience playing it and learning the concepts behind git, fossil
, version control in general. Its striking that we do not even have an
Indian code forge.
:::

The pattern is consistent:

> Commercial Pressure ↳ Internal Build ↳ Open-Source Release ↳ Ecosystem
> Adoption → next cycle
>
> China has built a flywheel for foundational software.

This led to a set of questions:

> 1.  Are we building databases from scratch in India?
> 2.  Are we building anything of foundational nature in India as far as
>     software is concerned?

My first check was UPI --- India\'s most celebrated technology success.

::: questions
**Q1: What transaction volume in TPC-C terms would UPI handle?**

UPI processed

-   \~500 million transactions/day (2024 average)
-   \~20 billion/month, \~645 million/day (Aug 2025)

Average throughput:

-   \~3,729 transactions per second (TPS) (IBEF 2023).
-   That is \~224,000 TPM --- roughly comparable to a mid-tier
    single-node TPC-C submission. PolarDB Limitless sustains \~2,055
    million TPM (≈34 million TPS) --- a gap of roughly 9,000×. (TPC-C
    measures a weighted multi-transaction mix, not single payments; the
    comparison is approximate.)

**Q2: What is the reported error volume in UPI?**

NPCI reports a technical decline rate (system-side failures, not user
errors like wrong PIN) of \~0.3--0.5%. Total decline rate including user
errors is \~5--8% depending on the bank. NPCI publishes monthly
dashboards with bank-wise success rates; most PSPs exceed 96% success.

**Q3: What database does UPI use?**

NPCI has not publicly disclosed the database backing the UPI switch.
Industry sources indicate Oracle on IBM infrastructure for the core
clearing system. Participating banks (\~300+) use their own core banking
databases --- Oracle, SQL Server, and various CBS vendors. There is no
publicly available evidence of an Indian-built database underpinning
UPI.

**Q4: Where does the UPI transaction load live --- central clearance or
participating nodes?**

UPI load is distributed across the network:

-   Authentication (MPIN/UPI PIN): at the PSP bank\'s servers
-   Fund validation and debit/credit: at remitter and beneficiary bank
    core banking systems (\~300+ bank nodes)
-   Routing, clearing, and settlement: at NPCI\'s central UPI switch

NPCI central handles routing of all 500M+ daily transactions but the
heavy database operations (account lookup, debit, credit) happen at
individual bank nodes. The central switch is stateless for most flows.
:::

NPCI\'s DB requirement is structurally different from Ant\'s. The heavy
operations --- balance lookup, debit, credit --- sit at the \~300
participating bank nodes. NPCI central routes and settles but does not
own the transaction record. Ant owns every transaction end-to-end on its
own infrastructure; NPCI does not.

Even so, the NPCI switch routes 500M+ transactions daily; the
concurrency at that layer is not trivial. I expected architectural
cleverness at the switch --- something with a stated roadmap toward zero
foreign-tech dependency. Looking deeper, one reference surfaced:
[]{#O1_YUGBYT}[YugabyteDB](https://www.yugabyte.com/about/) at NPCI.

The closest reference found: Mindgate Solutions, UPI\'s largest Payment
Service Provider (PSP), runs on YugabyteDB --- reported at 9 billion
transactions per month
[source](https://www.yugabyte.com/success-stories/mindgate-solutions/).
Whether that figure covers one cluster or aggregates across Mindgate\'s
network is not publicly disclosed.

Our search for \"What India is building ?\" did not yield much but we
did observe

NPCI has begun open-sourcing. Two known contributions:

-   Falcon: Helm-chart templates for Hyperledger Fabric (HLF) on
    Kubernetes. Deployment automation; no core Fabric logic changed.
-   Drunix: Architectural fork of HLF --- new peer roles, plugs in
    YugabyteDB as distributed storage backend. More foundational.

We do have references to YugabyteDB , which is near foundational work
when compared to likes of the Chinese DB\'s mentioned in [Section
3.2](#3.2)

YugabyteDB --- the database doing the actual UPI-scale work --- is
Indian-origin, redomiciled to the United States. That pattern has a name
and its own section: [Section 6.4.4.1](#6.4.4.1).

::: story
The problem every database faces at scale:

-   One machine holds all the data.
-   One machine fails, all data is unavailable.
-   One machine fills up, the system is stuck.

The solution is distribution. Distribution requires consensus: agreement
on what was written and in what order. Where that agreement happens is
the architectural choice.

**Sharding:** divide the dataset across machines by a key --- hash or
range. Each machine owns one subset. Route reads and writes to the right
machine. Replicate each subset for resilience.

Family 1 --- Filesystem-level (PolarDB, Aurora, AlloyDB):

-   Data stored as pages (B-tree blocks, 8 KB) on a distributed
    filesystem.
-   All compute nodes share one storage pool.
-   Consensus at the page level --- which page, which order.
-   One node writes (primary). Multiple nodes read (replicas).
-   PolarDB Limitless stacked a sharding coordinator on top to break the
    single-writer ceiling --- two architectures combined.

Family 2 --- Tablet-level (YugabyteDB, CockroachDB):

-   Data sharded into tablets, each replicated across nodes.
-   Rows encoded as key-value pairs in RocksDB --- a sorted
    log-structured store with no query engine of its own.
-   Consensus via Raft: every write confirmed by quorum before
    acknowledgement to the client.
-   Both reads and writes scale horizontally.

YugabyteDB\'s specific choice:

-   SQL query layer: PostgreSQL --- parser, planner, executor ---
    untouched.
-   Storage layer: PostgreSQL heap replaced with RocksDB + Raft.
-   The engineering work: encoding PostgreSQL rows, types, and indexes
    into RocksDB key-value format.
-   Done before PostgreSQL 12\'s Table Access Method (TAM) API existed
    --- required patching PostgreSQL internals directly.
-   TAM solves storage abstraction on one node; it does not solve
    distribution.

CockroachDB followed the same family but went further: rewrote the SQL
engine in Go, wrote its own storage engine (Pebble). More original work;
same core insight --- leave the solved layer, attack the gap.
:::

The closest India has come to a database claim in this space is ShaktiDB
--- a PostgreSQL 17.4 fork from []{#O1_IITMPR}[IITM
Pravartak](https://pravartak.org.in/about-us/) and C-DAC (Centre for
Development of Advanced Computing), under
[]{#O1_MEITY}[MeitY](https://www.meity.gov.in/about-us) (Ministry of
Electronics and Information Technology) funding, released June 2025 (as
announced to the author; no public repository yet). It adds
[]{#O1_RBI}[RBI](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/AboutusDisplay.aspx),
[]{#O1_CERTIN}[Cert-In](https://www.cert-in.org.in/index.jsp), and
[]{#O1_SEBI}[SEBI](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/home/HomeAction.do?doListing=yes&sid=1&ssid=0&smid=0)
compliance wrappers on top of community PostgreSQL. It is not a new
storage engine or a new consensus layer. It is a hardened,
compliance-configured fork, deployed by a systems integrator into
captive government demand. ShaktiDB is examined in [Section
6.4.3](#6.4.3).

## 3.7. The Paradox {#3.7}

26.7 million developers. \$283bn in revenue. The second-largest
developer base by headcount, behind the US. 5.2 million new developers a
year. Run any model of how foundational software gets built and these
inputs predict a mature ecosystem of Indian-owned databases, brokers,
runtimes, kernels. The prediction fails. The count of globally adopted
foundational software projects originated and governed from India is
zero.

China stood at a comparable point a generation ago --- worse inputs on
most axes --- and built the floor anyway. The operative variable was not
developer headcount. It was whether a wall existed that could not be
rented around.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    I1["$283 bn — IT revenue / yr"]
    I2["26.7 mn — total developers"]
    I3["5.2 mn / yr — new developers"]
    I4["#2 — OSS contributors"]
    I1 & I2 & I3 & I4 --> EXP["Expected foundational software floor<br/><i>OS · databases · brokers · compilers · consensus — originated in India, globally adopted, neutrally governed</i>"]
    EXP --> OBS["Observed reality — globally adopted foundational software originated and governed from India<br/><b>≈ 0</b>"]:::zero
    classDef zero fill:#ffe8e8,stroke:#c22f4e,color:#c22f4e
```

# 4. What Type of Work Do We Do in India? {#4}

## 4.1. India's Software Story Is a Success {#4.1}

By every headline measure the Indian software industry is a success:
US\$283bn revenue, 5.80mn employed, 55% of the world\'s outsourced IT
delivery. The chart records these inputs. The question this essay asks
is why none of them produced a foundational output.

## 4.2. Success Is at the Application and Application Support Layer {#4.2}

The layers India occupies --- application and application-support ---
sit on top of others' runtimes, protocols, and databases. The dependency
is total; the value capture is thin.

\~79% of FY25 revenue is exports (\$224bn of \$283bn). 50.3% of that
goes to the US; 31.4% to Europe; 15.5% to the UK. Three anglophone
markets, one relationship: India writes and operates software that other
firms own, priced below what those owners would pay to build it at home.
What India sells is the cost gap, not the software. (NASSCOM FY25)

What India does not build is foundational software for domestic or
global consumption. There is no Indian-owned operating system that
powers a significant share of the world\'s servers, no Indian-owned
database in the TPC-C rankings, no Indian-owned message broker,
compiler, or consensus engine that the rest of the world depends upon.
The floor is rented, and the wallpaper is sold.

## 4.3. The Mental Model: Raw Material → Plumbing → Floor → Building → Interior {#4.3}

To make the argument precise, it helps to have a shared picture of what
software actually is. This essay uses a five-layer metaphor drawn from
construction:

-   **Raw Material.** The substrates that everything else is made from:
    operating-system kernels, programming languages, schedulers, build
    systems, runtimes, physical compute primitives (PTY/TTY, PHY,
    buffers), and hardware abstraction layers. These are the sand and
    cement of software.

-   **Plumbing and Utilities.** The pipes and wires that connect
    everything: protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP, gRPC), frameworks (Spring,
    React), message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ), terminals and shells,
    editors, serializers, and the abstractions built around data
    structures such as files, databases, and filesystems. These are not
    the foundation itself, but they are below the visible surface.

-   **The Floor.** The load-bearing infrastructure that applications
    stand on: database engines, OS distributions, consensus systems
    (Raft, Paxos implementations), service meshes, and container
    orchestrators. Whoever owns the floor sets the price, the roadmap,
    and the shutdown date for everyone above.

-   **The Building.** What a person actually uses: applications,
    dashboards, wallets, office suites, e-commerce platforms.

-   **Interior Decoration.** The work that keeps the building habitable:
    support, maintenance, incremental feature addition, customisation,
    and integration. This is where most of India\'s IT services revenue
    lives.

Dependency runs downward: nothing in the top row executes without every
box in the bottom row. Value capture runs upward: the closer you are to
the raw material, the harder you are to replace and the more of the
value chain you capture. India\'s named assets attach almost exclusively
to the top two tiers.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["Interior — support, maintenance, feature addition, integration<br/><b>PRESENT</b> — 55% global share"]:::present
    B["Building — Zoho, Freshworks, Flipkart, PhonePe, Paytm<br/><b>PRESENT</b> — export-first"]:::present
    C["The Floor — DB engines, OS distros, consensus, meshes, orchestrators<br/><b>ABSENT</b> — ≈ 0 globally adopted"]:::absent
    D["Plumbing — protocols, MQs, frameworks, terminals, shells, serializers<br/><b>MINIMAL</b> — Kitty, kaf-relay"]:::minimal
    E["Raw Material — kernels, languages, compilers, schedulers, runtimes, PHY<br/><b>ABSENT</b> — no Indian LLVM, no Indian Linux distro"]:::absent
    A --- B --- C --- D --- E
    classDef present fill:#e8f5ee,stroke:#008a6d,color:#008a6d
    classDef absent fill:#fdecef,stroke:#c22f4e,color:#c22f4e
    classDef minimal fill:#fdf6f2,stroke:#b07a10,color:#b07a10
```

## 4.4. Hypothesis Refined: Based on Resource-Based View (RBV) {#4.4}

Jay Barney's Resource-Based View: competitive advantage accrues to
assets that are Valuable, Rare, Inimitable and Non-substitutable (VRIN)
--- properties that concentrate at the bottom of the software stack. A
database engine qualifies on all four (everything runs on it; few can
build one; a decade to harden; you cannot swap Oracle for a spreadsheet
at scale). A customer-support chatbot is valuable but fails the other
three.

India does not own the VRIN assets in software. It owns the application
layer, which is valuable but not rare. It rents the floor, paying in
licence fees, cloud bills, talent drain, and strategic vulnerability.
The rent is not merely financial. Every year the floor stays foreign,
the domestic capability to build it atrophies further, because no one
learns to pour concrete they can buy ready-mixed.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["Application<br/>Valuable ✓ · Rare ✗ · Inimitable ✗ · Non-sub ✗<br/><b>India present</b>"]:::app
    B["The Floor<br/>Valuable ✓ · Rare ✓ · Inimitable ✓ · Non-sub ✓<br/><b>India rents</b>"]:::floor
    C["Raw Material<br/>Valuable ✓ · Rare ✓ · Inimitable ✓ · Non-sub ✓<br/><b>India rents</b>"]:::floor
    A --- B --- C
    classDef app fill:#f7f9fc,stroke:#8595a6,color:#8595a6
    classDef floor fill:#fdecef,stroke:#c22f4e,color:#c22f4e
```

## 4.5. DPI: The Protocol & Mandate Floor (India's Parallel Path) {#4.5}

An honest objection first: India has built world-class digital
infrastructure --- UPI (\~₹314 lakh crore a year (FY26, NPCI), \~48.5%
of the world's real-time payments, ACI Worldwide 2023), Aadhaar
(\~1.39bn enrolled), ONDC (opening e-commerce protocols at national
scale). These are real and not trivial.

But they are a *protocol floor*, not a *software-engineering floor*.
India built APIs, data standards, and identity layers. It did not build
the databases, runtimes, and message brokers on which those protocols
themselves run. The UPI switch routes 500M+ transactions daily; the core
clearing system is reported to run on Oracle on IBM infrastructure. The
protocol is Indian. The engine beneath it is not.

This distinction is the honest counter-thesis to the essay's central
claim, and engaging it strengthens rather than weakens the argument.
India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) is world-class at the
protocol and application layers. It does not extend to the layer
beneath. China built the engine *and* the protocol; India built the
protocol and rented the engine.

-   **UPI (Unified Payments Interface).** A real-time payment system
    developed by NPCI that enables instant money transfer between bank
    accounts through mobile devices. It defines the protocol --- the
    message format, the authentication flow, the settlement rules. It
    does not define the database that stores the ledger, the operating
    system that runs the servers, or the message broker that queues
    transactions. Those are purchased or rented.

-   **ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce).** A network-centric
    protocol for e-commerce that aims to break platform monopolies by
    enabling decentralized discovery and transaction. Like UPI, it is a
    set of standards and APIs. The implementation --- the search index,
    the payment gateway, the logistics orchestrator --- is left to
    private participants, most of whom run on foreign foundational
    software.

-   **ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account).** A free, voluntary
    14-digit unique health identifier that enables citizens to digitally
    store, manage, and share medical records with verified healthcare
    providers. It is a standard and an identity layer. The electronic
    health record systems that consume ABHA numbers, the databases that
    store them, and the networks that transmit them are built on foreign
    software stacks.

Key references on India's DPI strategy:

-   Tigerfeathers, *"The Internet Country"* --- on how India built
    protocol-level digital infrastructure without owning the software
    floor beneath it.
-   iSPIRT Foundation, research papers on the India Stack and DPI
    approach --- documenting the strategic choice to build open
    protocols rather than proprietary systems.
-   NPCI annual reports and UPI transaction dashboards --- for volume
    and technical-decline data.

The DPI argument is not that India built nothing. It is that India built
one kind of floor --- protocol and mandate --- while omitting the other
kind --- software engineering. Both are necessary for strategic
autonomy. Owning the protocol without owning the engine is like owning
the railway gauge but importing the locomotive.

# 5. The Comparison: Data and Evidence {#5}

## 5.1. Compare at Each Layer --- What Tools Have Come from India? {#5.1}

Using the mental model from [Section 4.3](#4.3), we can now compare
India and China layer by layer. The comparison is not an indictment of
India\'s software industry --- it is a diagnosis.

The categories are the same ones used to describe the stack:

-   **Raw Material:** Kernels, languages, compilers, schedulers,
    runtimes.
-   **Plumbing:** Protocols, message queues, frameworks, serializers.
-   **The Floor:** Database engines, operating system distributions,
    consensus systems, container orchestrators.
-   **The Building:** Applications, SaaS products, consumer-facing
    services.

China has significant, globally recognised projects in every layer below
the building. India has almost none. The table that follows lists
representative projects from each country at each layer. The signal is
not that India lacks developers or revenue --- we have already conceded
both --- but that the output of that talent and revenue at the
foundational layers is structurally different in the two countries.

The gap is not a matter of a few missing projects. It is a matter of a
missing layer.

## 5.2. Establish: There Is Not Much Foundational Software from India {#5.2}

### 5.2.1. Dig Deeper --- Is It Really the Case? {#5.2.1}

The comparison table has \"None\" in several India cells. India\'s
foundational work is less visible --- not in TPC rankings, not in global
foundations. The known exceptions:

**PhonePe Drove:** Container orchestrator built to replace Mesos,
open-sourced but with low external contribution ([Section 6.7](#6.7)).

**kaf-relay:** Kafka relay tool from Zerodha, open-sourced but with few
PRs.

**DungBeetle:** Distributed job server in Go for asynchronous SQL read
jobs (reports) against MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse. Built at Zerodha
to manage their reporting layer. Open-sourced but with low external
adoption.

**Kitty:** Terminal emulator by Kovid Goyal (Indian-born). Its own
protocol, extension system, and remote control. Widely used but driven
by a single maintainer.

**Zoho/AdventNet:** Started with open-source Java SNMP API and WebNMS
framework; later pivoted to proprietary enterprise products. Covered in
[Section 5.2.2](#5.2.2).

**YugabyteDB:** Indian-origin distributed SQL database, re-domiciled to
the US. Covered in [Section 6.4.4.1](#6.4.4.1).

These are real projects. They are also exceptions. They do not form an
ecosystem. The table that follows documents their status, and the
analysis in [Section 6](#6) examines why they did not scale into a
domestic foundational software industry.

  Layer      Project         Details
  ---------- --------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Floor      PhonePe Drove   Distributed container orchestrator (replaced Mesos)`<br>`{=html}Apache 2.0`<br>`{=html}Maintained; low community
  Floor      DungBeetle      Async SQL job server in Go; Zerodha`<br>`{=html}MIT`<br>`{=html}Maintained; low community
  Floor      WebNMS          Network management framework; Zoho`<br>`{=html}Proprietary`<br>`{=html}Active; internal to Zoho
  Floor      Zoho OS/DB      In-house OS and database for Zoho products`<br>`{=html}Proprietary`<br>`{=html}Active; internal to Zoho
  Floor      YugabyteDB      Distributed SQL, PostgreSQL wire protocol`<br>`{=html}Apache 2.0`<br>`{=html}Active; re-domiciled to US
  Floor      ShaktiDB        PostgreSQL 17.4 fork; RBI/Cert-In/SEBI compliance`<br>`{=html}Open source`<br>`{=html}Active; captive govt deploy
  Plumbing   kaf-relay       Kafka relay; Zerodha`<br>`{=html}MIT`<br>`{=html}Maintained; low community
  Plumbing   Kitty           Terminal emulator; own protocol + extension system`<br>`{=html}GPLv3`<br>`{=html}Active; single maintainer

  : Indian Foundational & Foundational-Adjacent Projects
  {#Tab.Indian_Foundational_List}

\"Low community\" means \<10 external contributors, \<50 PRs from
outside the originating organisation. \"Re-domiciled\" means
incorporated in the US to access funding and enterprise customers.
\"Captive govt deploy\" means used by government entities but without
broader market adoption.

### 5.2.2. The Exceptions --- Zoho/AdventNet Story {#5.2.2}

Zoho, known today as a SaaS and enterprise software company, began as
AdventNet in 1996. Founded in New Jersey, USA, by Sridhar Vembu and a
small team, the company started with fifteen people building a Java SNMP
(Simple Network Management Protocol) API. The product was open-source,
and it gained early traction in the network management community.

The SNMP API was followed by WebNMS, an open-source framework for
building network management applications. The early open-source approach
gave AdventNet visibility and credibility, but it was the proprietary
products built on top of that foundation --- ManageEngine --- that
provided sustainable revenue.

What distinguished AdventNet from most Indian software companies of the
era was that it was building its own stack. The SNMP API, the WebNMS
framework, and later the internal middleware, database, and operating
system were all self-developed. When the dot-com bust arrived in 2000,
AdventNet survived because it owned its floor --- it was not dependent
on vendor licenses or third-party platforms that could be withdrawn or
repriced.

The company later pivoted from selling frameworks to selling enterprise
applications (ManageEngine) and then cloud productivity tools (Zoho
Office). The floor --- the proprietary middleware, database, and OS ---
remained internal. The company grew, but the ecosystem did not. Zoho\'s
story is covered further in [Section 5.2.2](#5.2.2).

```{ojs}

//| label: fig-adventnet-timeline
//| fig-cap: "AdventNet / Zoho — 1996 to 2026"
{
const zoho_tl = [

AdventNet\'s early success came from selling network management
frameworks. But frameworks are tools for builders; the real money is in
the applications that builders create. The company gradually pivoted
from selling WebNMS to building its own enterprise applications ---
first ManageEngine (IT management) and then Zoho Office (productivity).

The pivot was strategic and successful. Zoho is now a profitable,
privately held company with over 100 million users worldwide (company
claim, 2023). It builds its own OS, database, and middleware --- it owns
the floor.

But the floor is proprietary. It is not open-source. Zoho does not sell
its database or its middleware as products. The technology that gives
Zoho its cost advantage and operational flexibility is kept internal.

This is the key structural lesson: Zoho built a floor for itself, but it
did not build a floor for India. The company\'s success is individual,
not systemic. There is no Zoho ecosystem, no Zoho developer community,
no Zoho foundation that holds the IP for the public good. The floor is a
moat, not a commons.

The early open-source approach (Java SNMP API, WebNMS) seeded the
company. The proprietary pivot built the business. But the open-source
work was abandoned, and the proprietary work was not shared. India got a
successful company but not a foundational software ecosystem.

This pattern --- build open-source, pivot proprietary, keep the floor to
oneself --- is not unique to Zoho. It is one of the shapes of Indian
foundational work examined in [Section 6.4.3](#6.4.3).

## 5.3. What Indian Companies Are Actually Building? What Are Other Asian Economies Building? {#5.3}

India has produced several globally recognised software product
companies: Zoho, Freshworks, Postman, and BrowserStack. They are
successful by any measure --- revenue, users, brand recognition. But
their success follows a different pattern from their East Asian
counterparts.

The critical distinction is the primary market:

Indian product companies were built for export markets from the first
line of code. Their customers are in the United States and Europe. The
domestic market was not large enough or willing enough to pay for Indian
software products.

East Asian product companies --- Tencent, Alibaba,
[]{#O1_BAIDU}[Baidu](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/BIDU/) (China);
Rakuten, Line (Japan); Naver, Kakao (Korea) --- were built for their
domestic markets first. They expanded globally only after securing a
captive home base.

This distinction matters for foundational software. Building for the
domestic market first creates a forcing function: you must build for
local language, local regulation, local scale, and local infrastructure.
These requirements often cannot be met by off-the-shelf global products.
The domestic market becomes the wall that forces you to build your own
foundation.

Indian product companies, by contrast, build for global customers who
already use global infrastructure. There is no domestic forcing function
--- no reason to build a new database, a new operating system, or a new
message broker. The export-first model is efficient for product
companies but it does not generate foundational assets.

The exception proves the rule: Zoho, the essay\'s own flagship, is
export-first and yet built its own floor (OS, database, middleware).
Zoho\'s difference was founder discipline and the absence of VC pressure
--- a 20-year horizon most export-first companies lack ([Section
5.2.2](#5.2.2)).

  Country       Representative Companies                  Domestic Revenue   Primary Market
  ------------- ----------------------------------------- ------------------ ----------------
  China         Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, ByteDance        \~80--90%          Domestic
  Japan         Rakuten, Line, Mercari                    \~70--80%          Domestic
  South Korea   Naver, Kakao, Coupang                     \~70--80%          Domestic
  India         Zoho, Freshworks, Postman, BrowserStack   \~10--20%          Export (US/EU)

  : Asian Product Companies --- Domestic vs Export Markets
  {#Tab.Asian_Product_Comparison}

Sources: Company annual reports, industry analyses. Domestic revenue
share is approximate. East Asian companies derive the majority of
revenue from home markets, creating a forcing function for local
infrastructure investment. Indian companies are export-first, with no
captive domestic market to justify foundational investment.

## 5.4. Consumer Applications --- Messaging and Others {#5.4}

### 5.4.1. What Is Excluded, and Why {#5.4.1}

Firms that sell services rather than software are excluded --- their
internal tools are cost-reduction assets, not products. OceanBase and
TDSQL originated inside excluded firms; that story is in [Section
6](#6).

  Firm        Country   Primary Service      Rationale for Exclusion
  ----------- --------- -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------
  Alibaba     China     E-commerce / Cloud   Sells retail/cloud services; software is cost-reduction tool
  Tencent     China     Social / Gaming      Sells social/gaming services; software is internal asset
  Baidu       China     Search / AI          Sells search/advertising; software is internal asset
  Didi        China     Ride-hailing         Sells transportation; software is operational infrastructure
  ByteDance   China     Social / Content     Sells advertising/content; software is internal asset
  Flipkart    India     E-commerce           Sells retail services; no software product sold externally
  Swiggy      India     Food delivery        Sells delivery services; no software product sold externally
  Ola         India     Ride-hailing         Sells transportation; software is operational infrastructure
  Paytm       India     Payments / Fintech   Sells payment services; software is operational infrastructure

  : Excluded Firms --- Service Providers, Not Software Product Companies
  {#Tab.Excluded_Firms}

### 5.4.2. The Theory: How Consumer Apps Become Successful {#5.4.2}

1.  5.4.2.1. Consumer App Success Routes

    Consumer applications can succeed via two broad routes. These routes
    have different structural consequences for foundational software.

    The first route is the protocol route. Define a protocol that
    becomes a standard, and build an application that leverages it.
    WhatsApp used the Signal Protocol for end-to-end encryption. UPI is
    a national protocol for real-time payments. The value is in the
    protocol, not in the implementation. The protocol can be adopted by
    others; the implementation is a commodity.

    The second route is the engineering route. Build an application that
    is so well-engineered --- performance, user experience, features ---
    that it wins on merit, using open foundations. Signal built on
    open-source libraries but differentiated on engineering quality.
    Telegram differentiated on speed and features.

    The protocol route creates a floor at the standards level. It
    defines how systems interact. But it does not require building the
    underlying databases, operating systems, or networking stacks. The
    protocol is the floor; the implementation is rented.

    The engineering route creates a floor at the implementation level.
    It requires deep optimisation of the stack. It often forces the
    builder to modify or replace foundational components.

    India\'s consumer successes --- UPI, Aadhaar, ONDC --- are protocol
    successes. They define standards. India has not produced a globally
    successful consumer application that is engineering-led in the sense
    of deep stack ownership.

      Application   Primary Route   Foundation                 Notes
      ------------- --------------- -------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------
      WhatsApp      Protocol        Signal Protocol            Built on existing encryption protocol; acquired by Meta
      Signal        Engineering     Open-source libraries      Differentiated on privacy and engineering quality
      Telegram      Engineering     MTProto protocol           Differentiated on speed, features, cloud sync
      UPI           Protocol        NPCI specifications        National protocol; implementations are commodity
      ONDC          Protocol        Open network specs         National protocol; implementations are commodity
      Google Maps   Engineering     Proprietary infra          Differentiated on data quality and routing
      Baidu Maps    Engineering     Proprietary + state data   Differentiated on local data and integration

      : Consumer App Success Routes --- Protocol vs Engineering
      {#Tab.Consumer_App_Routes}

    ::: story
    The Unicorn That Rented the Floor

    The following is an illustrative, composite account --- it
    amalgamates several Indian consumer startups, not one named company.

    In 2015, a well-funded Indian food delivery startup raised over
    \$500 million from top-tier venture capital firms. It grew to 10
    million users, processed 1 million orders a day, and achieved
    unicorn valuation in under three years.

    The stack was standard: AWS for compute, MongoDB Atlas for the
    database, Kafka on AWS MSK for messaging, React Native for the
    mobile app, and Stripe for payments. Everything was rented. The
    company\'s \"innovation\" was the delivery logistics algorithm --- a
    Node.js service running on rented servers, querying a rented
    database, sending messages through a rented queue.

    In 2018, a competitor with a similar product but deeper pockets
    began a price war. The unicorn responded by slashing delivery fees.
    Unit economics went negative. The investors demanded growth; the
    company obliged by expanding to 50 cities, adding 10,000 delivery
    partners, and doubling its engineering team.

    Then the rent came due. AWS bills tripled as the company scaled.
    MongoDB Atlas costs outpaced revenue growth. The logistics algorithm
    was bottlenecked by the database, but every proposed fix required
    changing the schema --- which meant downtime, which meant losing
    customers to the competitor. The company could not optimise its
    stack because it did not own the stack.

    In 2019, the company was acquired for 10% of its peak valuation. The
    acquirer shut down the Indian operations, kept the delivery partner
    network, and rewrote the logistics algorithm on its own proprietary
    infrastructure.

    What failed was not the product. What failed was the business model.
    The company had no moat. The delivery logistics algorithm was a thin
    wrapper around rented infrastructure. The floor is a moat --- and
    they never owned it.
    :::

2.  5.4.2.2. Map Applications

    Mapping applications provide a useful case study for the \"renting
    the floor\" thesis. Maps are infrastructure: they combine satellite
    imagery, street data, traffic patterns, routing algorithms, and
    user-generated content. The stack is deep and the data is expensive
    to collect.

    India has several mapping offerings: MapMyIndia (Mappls), Ola Maps,
    and ISRO\'s Bhuvan. Each occupies a different position in the stack.

    **MapMyIndia (Mappls):** Privately held, predates Google Maps in
    India. Owns its own street data and POI (point of interest)
    database. But the underlying infrastructure --- the servers, the
    geocoding engine, the routing algorithms --- is partly built, partly
    rented. The application layer is Indian; the floor is mixed.

    **Ola Maps:** Built by Ola to reduce dependency on Google Maps. Uses
    OpenStreetMap data and self-collected data from Ola\'s fleet. The
    routing engine is proprietary. But the core stack is built on
    open-source foundations. Ola Maps is a cost-reduction exercise, not
    a product sold to others.

    **ISRO Bhuvan:** Government-run, uses ISRO\'s satellite imagery. The
    data is sovereign --- India owns its own satellite pictures of its
    own territory. But the user interface, the API, and the developer
    ecosystem are weak. Bhuvan is a demonstration, not a product.

    Contrast with China\'s Baidu Maps and Russia\'s Yandex Maps. Both
    own their own satellite imagery, street data, traffic data, routing
    engine, and developer API ecosystem. The entire stack --- data,
    infrastructure, application --- is sovereign.

    The Indian mapping ecosystem is fragmented. MapMyIndia owns data but
    not the full infrastructure. Ola Maps owns infrastructure but only
    for internal use. ISRO owns satellite data but not the application
    layer. No single entity owns the full stack. The floor is rented in
    pieces.

      Map App               Origin   Pricing          Data Source                    Infrastructure            Usability / Ecosystem
      --------------------- -------- ---------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------- ------------------------------------------
      Google Maps           US       Freemium (API)   Satellite, street, user-gen    Full stack (Google)       Excellent; extensive developer ecosystem
      MapMyIndia (Mappls)   India    Commercial       Self-owned street/POI data     Mixed (data owned,        Good for enterprise; weak consumer
                                                                                     infra partly rented)      ecosystem
      Ola Maps              India    Internal (Ola)   OSM + Ola fleet data           Proprietary routing;      Internal only; not a product
                                                                                     open-source foundations   
      ISRO Bhuvan           India    Free (govt)      ISRO satellite imagery         Data sovereign;           Poor UX; no developer ecosystem
                                                                                     application weak          
      Baidu Maps            China    Freemium (API)   Own satellite/street/traffic   Full stack (Baidu)        Good; integrated with Baidu ecosystem
      Yandex Maps           Russia   Freemium (API)   Own satellite/street/traffic   Full stack (Yandex)       Good; integrated with Yandex ecosystem

      : Map Applications Comparison --- Data, Infrastructure, and
      Ownership {#Tab.Map_App_Comparison}

    Pattern: China and Russia have full-stack map applications --- data,
    infrastructure, and application owned by a single entity. India has
    fragmented ownership with no single entity owning the full stack.

## 5.5. Innovation Hub Data (from the attached PDF) {#5.5}

The layer comparison and product analyses in the preceding sections are
qualitative. They show patterns but do not quantify the systemic
differences between India and China in innovation capacity.

The key indicators are:

-   **R&D spending as a percentage of GDP:** Measures the scale of
    investment in research and development. Higher R&D intensity
    correlates with more foundational research and more deep-tech
    startups.

-   **ICT patents filed:** Measures the output of applied research in
    information and communication technologies. Patents are a proxy for
    commercialisable innovation.

-   **Scientific publications and citations:** Measures the quality of
    academic research. Citations indicate impact.

-   **Returnee researchers:** Researchers who studied or worked abroad
    and returned. Returnees bring skills, networks, and knowledge of
    global best practices.

India lags behind China in all four metrics. China\'s R&D/GDP is 2.58%
(World Bank, 2023), while India\'s is 0.65% (2020, latest available).
China\'s patent output is \~18× higher (WIPO 2023: \~1.64M vs \~90K
applications). China\'s returnee researcher population is larger and
more integrated into domestic institutions.

These metrics are not the cause of India\'s absence from the
foundational software floor. They are symptoms of the same underlying
condition: a governance system that does not prioritise long-term
investment in deep technology.

# 6. Why? {#6}

## 6.1. The Forcing Condition --- The Wall {#6.1}

Foundational software is not built for fun or for strategic planning
documents. It is built when existing solutions fail in a way that cannot
be fixed by paying more money, hiring more consultants, or waiting for
the vendor\'s next release. There are four kinds of walls:

1.  **Cost**. Licensing fees become unsustainable at scale.
2.  **Performance**. Off-the-shelf solutions cannot meet latency or
    throughput requirements.
3.  **Legal/Sovereignty**. Geopolitical risks or export restrictions
    force domestic alternatives.
4.  **Customisation**. The business requires deep integration that
    proprietary vendors cannot provide.

China faced all four walls and answered with greenfield sovereign
builds. India hit the same walls --- PhonePe (Mesos), Zerodha
(PostgreSQL) --- but answered by assembly and renting, not by building
the floor.

  Wall Type           China                                                                           India
  ------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Cost                Oracle licensing at Singles\' Day scale was cost-prohibitive                    Indian enterprises could afford licenses
  Performance         Alipay scale exceeded off-the-shelf DB limits; required custom storage engine   UPI\'s \~3,729 TPS average (2023) --- peak \>10,000 TPS (NPCI, Oct 2024) --- is within PostgreSQL/YugabyteDB capabilities
  Legal/Sovereignty   US-China trade war forced domestic alternatives                                 No comparable geopolitical pressure
  Customisation       Ant needed to modify storage engine; no vendor would accept feature requests    Indian enterprises customise at application layer, not infrastructure

> India hit walls, but answered by assembly and renting. China hit walls
> and was forced to build greenfield.

```{mermaid}
graph TD

    C --> D1[Cost<br/>Licensing unsustainable]

    C --> D3[Legal/Sovereignty<br/>Geopolitical restrictions]

## 6.2. The Patterns: How Foundational Software Gets Built {#6.2}

### 6.2.1. List Important Open-Source Projects {#6.2.1}

To understand how foundational software gets built, we need a canonical
list of projects that have succeeded. Each project demonstrates one or
more recurring patterns.

  Software       Description                                                     Floor~BuildingDevelopmentPattern~
  -------------- --------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------
  SQLite         Embedded DB, zero-config; Hipp, US Navy contract                Lone obsessive
  Linux          OS kernel; Torvalds, University of Helsinki                     Lone obsessive + Mass community
  Git            Version control; Torvalds, personal need                        Lone obsessive
  Nginx          Web/proxy server; Sysoev, C10K internal problem                 Specialist tool + Scale problem
  Redis          In-memory data store; Sanfilippo, personal need                 Lone obsessive
  PostgreSQL     RDBMS; UC Berkeley, DARPA-funded research                       Institutional commission + Mass community
  Apache httpd   Web server; Apache Software Foundation                          Mass community
  Kubernetes     Container orchestration; Google → CNCF                          Institutional commission
  LLVM           Compiler infrastructure; University of Illinois                 Institutional commission
  TCP/IP         Network protocols; UC Berkeley, DARPA-funded                    Institutional commission
  The Web        HTTP/HTML; Berners-Lee, CERN                                    Institutional commission + Mass community
  R              Statistical computing; University of Auckland                   Institutional commission + Specialist tool
  OpenSSL        Cryptography library; solo developers → community               Lone obsessive + Mass community
  OceanBase      Distributed RDBMS; Alibaba → Ant Group, Singles\' Day forcing   Institutional commission + Scale problem
  Hadoop         Distributed compute; Yahoo!, Google GFS/MapReduce scale         Institutional commission + Scale problem

  : 15 Canonical Foundational Open-Source Projects --- author\'s
  analysis of genesis conditions [*Author\'s Judgement*]{.spurious-link
  target="D1_AJ"} {#Tab.15_Canonical_Projects}

### 6.2.2. Analyze a Few {#6.2.2}

::: story
**SQLite: The Lone Obsessive**

In 2000, D. Richard Hipp was working on a US Navy contract to build a
database for guided missile destroyers. The requirements were strict:
the database had to be small, self-contained, reliable, and work without
a server. Hipp wrote a single C file that implemented a complete SQL
database engine. He released it to the public domain.

SQLite is now the most deployed database on Earth. It runs in every
Android phone, every iPhone, every web browser (via WebSQL), and
billions of embedded devices. The code is still maintained primarily by
Hipp and a small team.

What made SQLite possible was not a large corporation or a government
mandate. It was a single developer with a clear problem, deep expertise,
and the discipline to keep the code simple. The US Navy provided the
funding and the requirement; Hipp provided the execution.

SQLite exemplifies the "lone obsessive" pattern: a single individual
with a clear vision and the freedom to execute it.
:::

::: story
**PostgreSQL: Institutional + Community**

In 1986, Michael Stonebraker at []{#O1_UCBRKL}[UC
Berkeley](https://www.berkeley.edu/about/) received
[]{#O1_DARPA}[DARPA](https://www.darpa.mil/about) funding to build a
database system that would extend the relational model beyond simple
data types. The project was called POSTGRES. It introduced concepts like
object-relational extensions, rule systems, and procedural languages.

The research produced a working system, but the university did not
commercialise it. The code was released to the community. A group of
developers formed the PostgreSQL Global Development Group and continued
development, transforming it into a production-grade database.

PostgreSQL is now one of the most advanced open-source databases in the
world. It powers millions of applications, from startups to enterprises.
The community is large and distributed, but the core governance remains
meritocratic.

PostgreSQL exemplifies the "institutional + community" pattern: a
research project that outlived its funding by becoming a community
asset.
:::

### 6.2.3. Theorize: Five Recurring Patterns {#6.2.3}

From the canonical list, five recurring patterns emerge:

These patterns are not mutually exclusive. India\'s absence from
foundational software can be understood by examining which patterns are
present and which are absent.

  Floor~BuildingDevelopmentPattern~        Definition                                                                     Canonical Examples
  ---------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ -----------------------------------
  Lone obsessive                           Single individual or small team builds core out of personal need/curiosity     SQLite, Redis, Git
  Mass community                           Large distributed community grows around shared need, often corporate-backed   Linux, Apache httpd
  Institutional commission                 Corporation, government, or university funds development for internal use      Kubernetes, OceanBase, TCP/IP
  Specialist tool                          Built to solve specific niche problem; often by company or researcher          Nginx, LLVM
  Scale problem that refuses workarounds   Problem so large that no existing solution works, forcing new build            OceanBase (Singles\' Day), Hadoop

  : Five Floor~BuildingDevelopmentPatterns~ {#Tab.Five_Patterns_Table}

### 6.2.4. Story Box: Kubernetes & OceanBase --- The Institutional Commission {#6.2.4}

::: story
**Kubernetes and OceanBase: Institutional Commission**

[]{#T1_KUBERN}[Kubernetes](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes)
began as
[]{#O1_GOOGLE}[Google](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/GOOGL/)'s
internal cluster management system, Borg. Google had a scale problem:
millions of containers, petabytes of data, and thousands of developers.
No existing solution worked. Google built Borg, then open-sourced
Kubernetes. The project was donated to the
[]{#O1_CNCF}[CNCF](https://www.cncf.io/about/who-we-are/), a neutral
foundation, ensuring global adoption.

OceanBase began inside Alibaba in 2010; Ant Financial adopted it later.
The Singles' Day load broke Oracle's vertical scaling limits. Ant built
a distributed database from scratch. The project was open-sourced in
2021 under MulanPubL-2.0 (relicensed Apache-2.0, March 2026).

Both fit the institutional-commission pattern: a scale problem no vendor
could solve, then open-sourcing to win community adoption.

The parallel to India is stark. Indian corporations with scale problems
---NPCI, Zerodha, PhonePe---have built internal tools (Drove, kaf-relay,
DungBeetle), but they have not donated them to neutral foundations or
built communities around them. The institutional commission pattern
exists in India, but it stops at the internal-use stage.
:::

## 6.3. Revisit India and China List --- Add the Five Patterns {#6.3}

  Floor~BuildingDevelopmentPattern~   China (Projects)                                              India (Projects)               Why India Stalled
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------
  Lone obsessive                      None (or minimal)                                             Kitty (Kovid Goyal)            No foundation, no ecosystem; single maintainer ceiling
  Mass community                      Huawei (top-10 Linux kernel contributor), RocketMQ (Apache)   None                           No Indian-led mass community OSS project originated
  Institutional commission            OceanBase, TDSQL, PolarDB                                     Drove, kaf-relay, DungBeetle   Never donated to neutral foundation; stayed internal
  Specialist tool                     TiDB, openGauss, Tongsuo                                      None                           No Indian specialist tool reached external adoption
  Scale problem                       OceanBase (Singles\' Day), Alibaba MaxCompute                 None                           Scale problems solved by buying or renting, not building

  : Floor~BuildingDevelopmentPatterns~ --- India vs China
  {#Tab.India_China_Pattern_Mapping}

## 6.4. The Story of Gitee {#6.4}

Gitee (码云) was launched in 2013 by OSChina.net --- China\'s existing
open-source community and news portal. Not a lone-obsessive project: it
emerged from an existing developer community that needed a domestic
alternative to GitHub after it became inaccessible.

**Scale Metrics:**

-   Millions of repositories
-   Primary collaboration platform for Chinese developers
-   GVP (Gitee Most Valuable Project) certification
-   Interactive Git learning tools (learn-git-branching game)
-   Integration with Chinese cloud providers

**Top Gitee Projects (by Gitee ranking and GVP status):**

These projects are deeply embedded in China's domestic software
ecosystem and are not globally visible:

  Project        Category             Stars                                                                                                           Description
  -------------- -------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------
  Ruoyi (若依)   Enterprise/Backend   Enterprise Java framework (Spring Boot + Vue). Used as internal-system foundation across Chinese enterprises.   
  Sa-Token       Enterprise/Backend   Lightweight Java permission framework. Among highest-starred Java projects on Gitee.                            
  SpringBlade    Enterprise/Backend   Microservices architecture with SaaS multi-tenancy.                                                             
  1Panel         Infrastructure       Open-source server management panel.                                                                            
  openEuler      OS                   Huawei's enterprise Linux distribution. Hosted on Gitee.                                                        
  OpenHarmony    OS                   Huawei's sovereign OS kernel. Hosted on GitCode (migrated from AtomGit, 2025).                                  
  MindSpore      AI                   Huawei's AI computing framework. Hosted on Gitee.                                                               

**Observation 1: Chinese Language Dominance**

Gitee is overwhelmingly a Chinese-language platform. The code,
documentation, comments, and community discussions are in Chinese.
Projects like Ruoyi are built for Chinese enterprise needs---SSO
integrations with WeChat Work, DingTalk, Feishu; compatibility with
domestic chips/OS; Chinese regulatory compliance. This is not a
translation layer; it is a native ecosystem.

**Observation 2: The Strategic Ecosystem**

China is building a complete, native-language computing ecosystem:

  Layer                   Chinese Implementation
  ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Font rendering          Unicode, Harfbuzz, native font support
  IDEs                    Chinese-language programming environments (e.g., \"中文代码汉语编程\")
  Programming languages   Wenyan-lang (文言文编程), Chinese syntax languages
  Documentation           Chinese-first; English translations secondary
  Code hosting            Gitee → AtomGit
  AI compute              Model hosting + free GPU/NPU compute
  Governance              OpenAtom Foundation (state-backed, neutral)

**Secondary pointer: AtomGit as Evolution**

[]{#T1_ATOMGT}[AtomGit](https://atomgit.com/) --- operated by the
[]{#O1_OPNATM}[OpenAtom Foundation](https://openatom.org/en/about)
(state-backed, neutral governance) --- is the next layer: Code + Model +
Compute as an integrated service. openEuler and Ascend are migrating
there (OpenHarmony moved to GitCode in 2025). The foundation structure
means no single company can shut it down or pivot it commercially. India
has no equivalent institution.

::: story
**Gitee: China's Domestic Forge**

Gitee received state backing and integration with government
initiatives. By 2020, Gitee had overtaken GitHub in terms of the number
of Chinese developers using it as their primary platform.

Gitee is not just a hosting platform. It includes code review tools,
project management, DevOps pipelines, and a package repository. It is
integrated with Chinese cloud providers and government infrastructure.
It is the foundation of China's domestic software supply chain.

The existence of Gitee has two effects. First, it ensures that Chinese
open-source projects are not dependent on foreign platforms. Second, it
creates a captive audience for Chinese projects: developers who use
Gitee are more likely to discover and adopt other Chinese open-source
projects.

India has no Gitee. Indian developers host their projects on foreign
platforms. The domestic software supply chain is rented.
:::

### 6.4.1. Why Don't We Have an Indian Code Hosting Platform? {#6.4.1}

India has no domestic Git forge. Why?

Building a Git forge is not technically challenging---Gitea and GitLab
are open-source and can be self-hosted. The challenge is adoption:
getting millions of developers to use it. This requires either a "lone
obsessive" builder (like Linus Torvalds for Git) or institutional
backing (like China\'s support for Gitee).

India has neither. The market is too fragmented, and the government has
not prioritised this. The result is dependence on foreign platforms,
which poses risks for sovereignty and data security.

The absence of a domestic forge is a governance failure, not a technical
one.

### 6.4.2. Is This Because of the Hyped Jugaad Culture? {#6.4.2}

India did not fail to build foundational software because of Jugaad. It
did not build because it did not need to --- the floor was available to
rent. That was rational. Rational choices in one period become strategic
liabilities in the next when the landlord changes the terms.

::: story
**C-DAC and Huawei --- Same Era, Different Outcomes**
